title: MB8-26499
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) dismisses the appeal and confirms the determination that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, his wife XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and their daughter XXXX XXXX XXXX, are neither refugees within the meaning of the United Nations Convention relating to the Status of Refugees (the Convention) nor persons in need
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, his wife XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and their daughter XXXX XXXX XXXX, for whom Mr. XXXX XXXX is the designated representative, are citizens of Mexico. They left their country following apparent death threats related to the perception by some individuals that Mr. XXXX XXXX father was a member of a rival criminal group. Aside from the threats alleged, one of his brothers reportedly died in a suspicious manner while detained by the police. Another brother was allegedly involved in a suspicious motor vehicle accident. As a result, he allegedly left Mexico in March 2018 to come to Canada.

The Refugee Protection Division (RPD) found that Mr. XXXX XXXX credibility was undermined because he did not seek government protection and failed to establish a nexus of conspiracy and collusion between the police and some cartels who begrudged his family.

He appealed against the decision of the RPD on November 19, 2018, alleging that: - the credibility finding was drawn arbitrarily without considering the facts before it; - it erred by making a generally negative credibility finding; and - it breached the principles of natural justice and procedural fairness in assessing the law and the facts by determining that Mr. XXXX XXXX is not a person in need of protection.

The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) dismisses the appeal and confirms the determination that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, his wife XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and their daughter XXXX XXXX XXXX, are neither refugees within the meaning of the United Nations Convention relating to the Status of Refugees (the Convention) nor persons in need of protection pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

The RAD reviews RPD decisions after carrying out its own analysis of the record by applying the correctness standard of review.1 The exception to this rule is that, where the RPD has a meaningful advantage, the RAD may show deference.2
paragraphs.heading_before: ROLE OF THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

paragraphs.text: I will apply the correctness standard as I carry out an independent analysis of the record, which includes all the evidence and listening to the recording.
The determinative issue is credibility.

Mr. XXXX XXXX father inadvertently found himself in the middle of a police raid of a cartel and was incarcerated for XXXX years as of 2008. His conviction was overturned in 2016 and the decision to release him was maintained by the Court of Appeal.

Mr. XXXX XXXX family allegedly received death threats after his father was arrested. These threats allegedly stopped until he was released, each cartel believing that his father was tied to the other.

In XXXX 2018, one of his brothers was allegedly arrested and XXXX XXXX XXXX in his cell. Mr. XXXX XXXX allegedly received a telephone threat six days later, and a second brother, also threatened by telephone, was allegedly involved in a motorcycle accident shortly after.

At first glance, it is important to note that Mr. XXXX XXXX claim was submitted with his father's, which was allowed. Was the Refugee Protection Division's credibility finding made arbitrarily without considering the facts before it?
The RPD noted that Mr. XXXX XXXX lived in Tocula from XXXX 2010 to 2016 without being threatened. He stayed there for two more years after his father was released and left.

One brother allegedly died in XXXX 2018 in circumstances that amount to XXXX. Six days later, Mr. XXXX XXXX was allegedly threatened by telephone that he would be next. Three weeks later, a second brother, who had also supposedly received telephone threats in the previous months, was knocked over by a truck when he was on a motorcycle with his spouse.
The ties between the threats received and the circumstances of the tragic events are the basis of his fear that led him to flee and claim refugee protection.

The RPD noted that: - no step had been taken with the police concerning the threat that he had received; - no evidence had been submitted to establish any collusion between the police and the cartels; and - the injuries inflicted on his brother from the motorcycle accident, reported in the medical evidence submitted, are not consistent with the extent of injuries alleged by Mr. XXXX XXXX in his account.

The memorandum of appeal states that it is unreasonable to require Mr. XXXX XXXX to provide clear and convincing evidence of the cartel's involvement in the death of his brother. According to the memorandum, listing enough indicators serves to establish irregularities that may be explained by the situation in which the family found itself when the father was incarcerated.

As such, he alleges that his brother's death XXXX XXXX was suspicious in that procedures ensuring his security, such as XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, were not followed. It was allegedly not the first incident of its kind at this police station.

Mr. XXXX XXXX alleges that he would be subjected to a risk to his life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment by criminals or police corrupted by cartels, working for them or cooperating with them and wanting to carry out threats.

However, the allegation of risk, of which his brother's death is proof, is contrary to the police investigations to shed light on his suicide, as indicated in the article submitted, drawn from the Internet site Noticieroaltavoz.com, Exhibit C-11 B.

Mr. XXXX XXXX did not take any steps in relation to these alleged threats. The conclusions about the absence of protection available are based on speculation about events linked to his two brothers. Nothing serves to establish that they were of interest to a criminal group.
First, his brother's arrest stemmed from his impaired driving, corroborated by the discovery of substances involved in the consumption of alcohol, as indicated in the autopsy report, Exhibit c-11 F.

With respect to his other brother, he did not apparently attribute significance to the numerous threats that he allegedly received a few months earlier. According to the medical certificate, Exhibit C-12A, his motorcycle accident left him with a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX hematoma requiring elective esthetic surgery. Nothing indicates that this accident was in relation to the alleged threats previously received.
There is no reason to question the events recounted by Mr. XXXX XXXX. However, they do not support a finding that the speculations made to explain their occurrence are credible.

Mr. XXXX XXXX fear of persecution by state agents working for criminal groups is not credible. The ties between the various incidents on which he bases his fear are pure speculation. His justification to explain the absence of steps by the police is unsatisfactory because it is based on speculations that are not credible.

The documentary evidence submitted establishes inadequate protection, not an absence of state protection. That said, Mr. XXXX XXXX was not required to establish that he had exhausted all options available in terms of protection but rather that he had taken all reasonable measures in the circumstances. This is done by taking into account the general situation in Mexico, all the steps actually taken and his relationship with the authorities.3

In this case, the harm that he alleged he faced was not credible and did not justify his actions. His situation did not prevent him from approaching the authorities, given the outcome in his father's case and the open investigations concerning the circumstances of his brother's tragic death. Without any history with the authorities, there is no reason why they would not help him. At the very least, in light of the above, he was obliged to take a concrete step in this respect.

As a result, the RPD's finding that Mr. XXXX XXXX credibility was undermined because he failed to go to the authorities for protection owing to speculation of collusion between the authorities and criminals is correct. It erred in its general negative credibility finding

The memorandum alleges that the RPD erred in making a general negative credibility finding. In doing so, it: - provided no explanation for ignoring the information in the National Documentation Package (NDP) on Mexico; and - relied on the concept of state protection without assessing whether it was objectively reasonable for Mr. XXXX XXXX to agree to avail himself of it.

The NDP on Mexico mentions many cases of institutionalized corruption, particularly regarding the relationship between the cartels and police forces. However, nothing in Mr. XXXX XXXX testimony supports a finding that the tragic and accidental events faced by his family are in relation to the criminal world. The reason for the threats, and their perpetrators, are unknown, and no step was taken to try to clarify their identity or the state's lack of willingness to provide protection.

The lack of a story for the two years following his father's departure, and the absence of a complaint by Mr. XXXX XXXX, based on speculation, undermine his credibility about the very existence of a risk to his life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.
The RPD did not find credible that the two events establish a conspiracy and collusion between the police and some cartels. I am of the opinion that this finding is correct.

The memorandum alleges that the RPD erred by identifying state protection as a determinative issue without presenting it clearly to Mr. XXXX XXXX during the hearing. However, it appears from the hearing that numerous issues regarding the possibilities of state protection and the recours available were raised. In addition, as shown, it was clearly indicated through the numerous questions asked on the matter throughout the hearing that this element was significant.

Furthermore, the memorandum states that the RPD should have considered the objective reasonsableness of Mr. XXXX XXXX obtaining state protection, considering his allegations that the state representatives were among the persecuting agents.

The incident involving state agents is linked to his brother's death in detention. Without Mr. XXXX XXXX taking steps with the state, exhibits C-11 B and C appear to indicate that the state decided to investigate his brother's death. At a minimum, such an act rather persuasively testifies to the existence of a system of investigations into the actions of state agents. I am of the opinion that the RPD's finding regarding the lack of general credibility and the absence of state protection are correct. Violation of the principles of natural justice and procedural fairness in assessing the law and the facts by determining that Mr. XXXX XXXX is not a person in need of protection
The third argument in the appeal is such that by making such a finding, the RPD violated the principles of natural justice and procedural equity in assessing the law and the facts.

Therefore, the argument made is such that the rejection of a claim under section 96 of the Convention by reason of an absence of credibility regarding subjective fear does not necessarily impact the objective nature of risk, pursuant to section 97.

The objective risk, faced Mr. XXXX XXXX and his family, allegedly stems from his relationship with his father, who is considered by each criminal group to be affiliated with the other camp, the death of a brother detained by the police following his arrest and the injuries inflicted on his other brother in a motorcycle accident. For Mr. XXXX XXXX, the intersection of these incidents is indicative of an objective risk.

However, initially, the risk of harm alleged by Mr. XXXX XXXX was not objective. It is a matter of two incidents affecting his family, of which the nexus with an alleged threat is tenuous. His brother's detention is objectively the result of his own actions. The state actor cannot be blamed for not fulfilling its duty. Furthermore, the circumstances stemming from his brother's death have been granted some importance by the state representatives who undertook an investigation. The second was allegedly involved in a highway accident. There is no evidence of the Mexican government's involvement in this case.

With respect to the argument of membership in the particular social group of family, in order for a refugee protection claim based on membership in a family to be allowed, the family member who is the main target of the persecution must be subjected to persecution owing to a reason set out in the Convention.4

Since Mr. XXXX XXXX father was determined to be a person in need of protection under section 97, his relationship cannot be the basis for a claim based on membership in the family given that he was not recognized under a Convention ground.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the determination that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXX, his wife XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXXand their daughter XXXX XXXX XXXXXXXXare not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection, under paragraph 111(1)(a) of the IRPA.
